subject: physics_2
question_text: Derive an expression for the intensity due to a point charge.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: E = F/Q₀ and F = (1/4πε₀)·QQ₀/d² give E = (1/4πε₀)·Q/d², directed along the force on a positive test charge, SI unit N C⁻¹. The book's heading 'Intensity if electric field' (printed p.20) is written correctly; the book defines E = F/Q then uses Q₀ — the test charge is Q₀ throughout here.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Definition of intensity
steps.mark_note: Force per unit positive test charge
lines: Intensity of electric field at a point is
the force experienced by a unit positive
test charge placed at that point.
where Q₀ is a small positive test charge.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words unit positive test charge are the definition.
steps.why: The field is defined through what it does to a charge, so the definition must name the probe: a unit, positive, test charge — small enough not to disturb the field it measures.
common_mistakes: Dropping the word positive. The direction of E is fixed by a POSITIVE test charge.
Writing E = FQ₀ instead of F/Q₀ — intensity is force PER charge.

recall.must_convey: That intensity is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/Q₀.
accept: E equals F by Q nought
force on a unit positive test charge
reject: one by four pi epsilon nought Q by d squared

steps.memory_tip: Definition first: E is force divided by the test charge that feels it.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: The charge Q at A, the test charge Q₀ at P, a distance d apart; F is the force on Q₀.
steps.why: The figure fixes the two points and the distance the derivation uses — Q at A, Q₀ at P, separation d — so the Coulomb force line that follows has its symbols already defined.
common_mistakes: Marking the distance from P back to itself or leaving d unlabelled — d is the full distance from A to P.

recall.must_convey: That the figure shows Q at A and the test charge Q₀ at P, a distance d apart, with the force F on Q₀.
accept: draw Q at A and Q nought at P
mark the distance d and the force arrow
reject: F equals Coulomb force by Q nought

steps.memory_tip: Source at A, probe at P, distance d — label all three before deriving.

steps.label: Force on the test charge
lines: Let a point charge Q be placed at a point
A. Place a test charge Q₀ at a point P at a
distance d from A. By Coulomb's law, the
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Coulomb's law applied to the pair Q and Q₀.
steps.why: The only physics input in this derivation is Coulomb's law — the field expression is that force with the probe divided out, so this line has to come first.
common_mistakes: Writing Q² or Q₀² in the numerator. The force involves the PRODUCT QQ₀.
Using r for the distance after the figure named it d — keep one symbol.

recall.must_convey: That the Coulomb force on the test charge is F = (1/4πε₀) · QQ₀/d².
accept: Coulomb force between Q and Q nought
one by four pi epsilon nought Q Q nought by d squared

steps.memory_tip: Write the ordinary Coulomb force first — the field comes from it in one division.

steps.label: Expression for E
lines: Intensity of the electric field at P is
The test charge Q₀ cancels: the field does
not depend on the charge used to test it.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Divide the force by Q₀ — the test charge cancels out.
steps.why: Dividing by Q₀ removes the probe from the answer. What remains depends only on the source charge Q and the distance d — that is what makes E a property of the point, not of the probe.
common_mistakes: Leaving Q₀ in the final expression. E must not contain the test charge.
Writing 1/d instead of 1/d² — the field inherits the inverse square from the force.

recall.must_convey: That dividing the force by Q₀ gives E = (1/4πε₀) · Q/d², with the test charge cancelled.
accept: E equals one by four pi epsilon nought Q by d squared

steps.memory_tip: One division and the probe disappears — E keeps only Q and d.

steps.label: Direction and unit
steps.mark_note: Direction of E and SI unit
lines: E acts along the force on the positive test
charge: away from Q if Q is positive, and
towards Q if Q is negative. Its SI unit is
steps.margin_note: Last mark. E is a vector — give its direction, then the unit.
steps.why: Intensity is a vector, so the derivation is complete only when the direction is stated. The direction follows from the positive test charge: pushed away by positive Q, pulled in by negative Q.
common_mistakes: Saying E always points away from the charge. That holds only when Q is positive.
Giving the unit as N/C² or C/N — it is newton per coulomb, N C⁻¹.

recall.must_convey: That E points along the force on a positive test charge — away from positive Q, towards negative Q — with unit N C⁻¹.

steps.memory_tip: Finish every field derivation the same way: direction, then unit.

insider_note: Four clean quarters: definition, Coulomb force, the division that cancels Q₀, then direction and unit — the last quarter is the one an answer written in a hurry leaves out.
